transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-19 08:00 PDT | Duration: ~57m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Park (Redwood SE), Erik Johansson (CTO), Lea Berg (ML lead), Simon Karlsson (Infra)

Summary (auto): Quick catalog walkthrough focused on open-model selection heuristics, how to map benchmarks to the compatibility matrix, and a plan for an internal benchmark run. Discussed Hosted vs Dedicated tradeoffs, VPC/peering concerns, SOC 2 and KMS questions. Agreed next steps for bench script and sample workload.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Maya with Redwood, this is Daniel our SE. good to meet you all.
[00:12] Erik: hey Maya, thanks. quick FYI, we only have about an hour, got a 9am sync after so if we can keep to that would be great.
[00:18] Maya: yeah totally, we'll run through the catalog heuristics, show the compatibility matrix and then land on a bench plan, cool?
[00:26] Lea: sounds perfect.
[00:29] Daniel: cool. so, um, starting with a high-level: Redwood's catalog groups open models by capability and runtime fit — so you can filter by sequence length, quantization friendliness, and kernel support — and we surface a compatibility score tied to latency & cost benches.
[00:44] Simon: when you say kernel support, you mean like vendor kernels? tigert, sorry.. (laughter) jk — um, like cuBLAS vs vendor specific?
[00:53] Daniel: yeah so it's more like, we pick optimized kernels based on architecture and hardware — there are mappings we maintain, sometimes we call it the kernel map, sometimes in docs it's kernel selection. it picks the best path for e.g. fp16, int8 quantized runtimes.
[01:08] Erik: are those mappings public or internal? we have to show some engineers.
[01:12] Daniel: they're internal but we can share a condensed compatibility matrix and a small explainer for your infra team — it won't leak proprietary heuristics but will show the model->hardware compatibility and expected relative perf.
[01:23] Lea: excellent. our two big concerns: latency SLOs for interactive features and cost per 1k tokens for higher throughput batch jobs.
[01:33] Maya: understandable. to be explicit — hosted API gives fastest time-to-value but less isolation, Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and more predictable throughput and VPC/networking options. there is also Redwood Private for fully customer-managed control plane if needed.
[01:47] Simon: On VPC — can we do VPC peering, or only private deployment? firewall wise we have strict egress policies.
[01:55] Daniel: we support VPC peering for Dedicated and Private options; for hosted customers we offer a private egress path via peering when you select a higher tier — Simon, we'll need your CIDR and allowed ports for the peering doc.
[02:08] Simon: got it, i'll add that to action items.

[02:15] Maya: quick demo — open the catalog, you'll see filters: token length distribution, target latency percentile, and quantization compatibility. we'll search for models suitable for short interactive chat and also for high-throughput summarization jobs.
[02:29] [Screen share noise / soft talking]
[02:35] Daniel: okay here i'm filtering for sequence length under 1k tokens, prefer quantization-friendly, hardware set to A100-ish, you can see a compatibility heatmap on the right — green is good, orange is workable, red is fallback.
[02:49] Lea: why is model-x listed orange even though it had great bench numbers in your public doc?
[02:56] Daniel: good call — sometimes the catalog score factors more than just raw bench TPS; it weighs kernel availability, KV cache behaviour for chat workloads, and how the model performs at shorter sequences. model-x's strengths are long-context throughput but it loses efficiency at shorter prefixes. also note some transcriptions earlier might show different model names — the autotagger can mismatch. apologies.
[03:15] Erik: KV cache? do you do prefix caching across requests?
[03:20] Daniel: yes, we support prefix/KV cache which helps chat loops — we cache key-value states to avoid re-computing earlier tokens; it reduces per-token cost and latency for repeated context. it's automatic for compatible models.
[03:31] Lea: is that preserved across restarts or ephemeral per session?
[03:35] Daniel: it's per-instance cache; for Dedicated we have options to persist short-lived cache shards to reduce warmup on scale outs, but it isn't a durable long-term store.

[03:44] Maya: shifting to benchmarks — we usually run three canonical benches: latency p50/p95 for interactive use, throughput (tokens/sec) for batch, and quality/regression on your prompts. for open models we include quantized runs e.g., int8 to estimate cost savings.
[03:59] Lea: are those bench artifacts reproducible? we want to run them in our environment as well.
[04:03] Daniel: yes, we'll provide a small runner script that runs the same prompts across model variants and outputs latency/cost CSVs; that's part of Daniel's action item.
[04:11] Simon: what about kernel versions and driver mismatch? last time we had a bench fluke due to driver/mini-driver mismatch.
[04:18] Daniel: good question — our bench runner locks expected CUDA and driver ranges; we also provide a compatibility matrix that lists recommended driver versions per kernel mapping. if you run in your infra we'll include a 'check' script that warns on mismatches.

[04:32] [05:00 marker, someone joins late but muted]
[05:12] Lea: okay about quality — we have a benchmark set of 300 prompts for product answers and 200 for summarization, but they skew long. is that okay?
[05:21] Daniel: totally — please share token distribution, it's helpful. for long prompts we might favor models with better long context kernels or ones that maintain effective KV scaling. sometimes there's a trade-off: best quality model can be 2x cost at your latency targets.
[05:36] Erik: we're okay paying for quality on critical paths but want to offload cheaper models for background tasks. can Redwood route by policy?
[05:44] Maya: yes — you can set smart routing policies: latency-first routing to a low-latency variant, or cost-priority routing that uses a cheaper quantized model and falls back on the high-quality model if either quality thresholds fail or latency spikes.
[05:58] Daniel: we also support canary rollouts and traffic splitting for model versioning. the console gives per-route metrics so you can judge quality/regression.

[06:10] Simon: security checklist — do you have SOC 2, SSO/SAML, KMS integration, and audit logs?
[06:17] Maya: yes, we are SOC 2 compliant, SSO via SAML/Okta supported, KMS/HSM integrations available for Dedicated/Private. audit logs are available in the console per request and per model, with retention options. i'll attach the SOC 2 summary and a security pack in the follow-up.
[06:33] Daniel: note that encryption at rest for model weights in Private deployments depends on how you configure your KMS. we can send a short doc on recommended KMS patterns.

[06:47] Lea: any notes on data retention for prompts? we need to ensure PII isn't stored for longer than our retention policy.
[06:54] Maya: by default Redwood does not persist prompts for hosted for more than 30 days unless configured; Dedicated/Private have controls so you can disable retention or route logs to your own storage. we'll include retention options in the security packet.

[07:06] [07:30 timestamp] Daniel: back to catalog heuristics — i want to highlight the 'compatibility band' concept: a model can be in the green band for A100 fp16 but orange for T4 int8 due to kernel/attention optimizations. the compatibility matrix shows these bands across hardware rows.
[07:24] Lea: do you include quantization accuracy deltas? e.g., rouge/qa metric drops after int8?
[07:30] Daniel: yes, for our curated models we include a delta column showing expected quality shift for quantized vs float runs using a small eval suite. it's rough but gives a direction.

[07:42] Erik: can you show an example mapping for our summarization workload?
[07:45] Daniel: sure — searching 'summarization' filter, here's model-A (green for A100 fp16, expected latency p95 220ms for 512 tokens), model-B (orange, great quality but higher cost), and model-C (green but more suited for long context, p95 450ms).
[07:59] Lea: i'm worried about p95 450ms for interactive; we target <300ms.
[08:04] Daniel: if <300ms is strict, we'll shortlist models that hit that on your sequence length distribution — model-A looks like the baseline. we'll also test quantized variants — sometimes int8 brings p95 down considerably.

[08:17] Maya: quick customer question — have you tried any open model with heavy compression/quantization in prod? what was the experience?
[08:24] Erik: we tried an int8 variant last year but saw visible quality regressions on summarization.
[08:29] Daniel: that's common; quantization-friendly architectures and calibration are key. our Optimize tooling suggests candidate models and quantization profiles that historically minimize quality regressions. we'll include a config suggestion in Daniel's runbook.

[08:42] Simon: how do you handle fallbacks when a quantized model hits a quality regression? is there automatic promotion to a float model?
[08:50] Daniel: yes, we support automatic fallback rules — you can set a quality threshold tied to synthetic evals; if the cheaper model fails it routes to the higher-quality variant. fallback latency will increase but keeps correctness.

[09:01] [09:30] Lea: for the bench run, will you run from your hosted infra or ours? we prefer running at least once from our infra to capture network egress and driver quirks.
[09:12] Daniel: the plan is twofold: we run a hosted-run to get baseline numbers and then you run the provided runner in your env. we'll coordinate config so outputs are comparable. the bench runner outputs same CSV schema.

[09:25] Maya: on pricing — we'll send a high-level hosted vs dedicated example: hosted token tiers vs dedicated reserved capacity per GPU hour. dedicated has commit discounts and lower per-token variance.
[09:37] Erik: any fine print on spot vs reserved? we need predictable throughput.
[09:41] Maya: dedicated gives reserved pools for predictable throughput; autoscaling policies and burst capacity are configurable. we'll include example autoscale configs in the pricing doc.

[09:52] Daniel: quick note about telemetry — Console will show per-route token counts, per-model latency and cost breakdown; you can export traces for a single request to see which kernel path was used. this helps debug kernel mismatch.

[10:06] Simon: do you surface which kernel was used for a request in the trace?
[10:09] Daniel: yes we include the kernel name and driver hints in the trace. sometimes the trace has truncated names due to transcription in the search, so don't worry if it looks odd in the demo.

[10:20] [11:00] Lea: ok, logistics — we'll provide prompt sets and a token distribution CSV. who should that go to?
[10:29] Maya: send to me and CC Daniel, we'll ingest and return a bench plan.
[10:34] Simon: about the VPC peering, are there NAT requirements? we run private subnets.
[10:38] Daniel: we can support private subnets with peering; we will list the required NAT rules in the peering doc.

[10:46] Maya: let's do a quick recap of what we'll send: pricing + SLA, SOC 2 + security packet, bench runbook + runner, compatibility matrix excerpt, and a short how-to for VPC peering.
[10:58] Erik: that covers it. timeline wise we want to present this to leadership on June 8th.
[11:04] Maya: great — we'll aim to have the materials so you can run an internal bench and have a follow-up by the first week of June.

[11:12] [11:30 wrap-up] Simon: small technical Q — if we want on-prem, what's the typical lead time?
[11:18] Daniel: on-prem varies — for a small pilot it's typically 6-8 weeks for packaging and validations; full air-gapped enterprise rollouts can take longer. we'll scope once we see your network constraints.

[11:30] Lea: do you support SAML groups mapping to RBAC in the console?
[11:34] Maya: yes, SAML group mapping and role-based access control are supported.

[11:38] Erik: final ask — can Daniel include an example CSV output from a bench run so we know what to expect?
[11:43] Daniel: yes, sample CSV and a short parser script included in the runbook.

[11:48] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the docs and action items.
[11:54] Erik: thanks, appreciate it.
[11:57] Meeting ends.

Post-call recap (auto): Action items noted above. Primary focus: confirm VPC networking, share prompts and token distribution, Redwood to deliver bench runbook and pricing. Follow-up 30m bench kickoff scheduled pending customer availability week of 2026-05-25.
